newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-LEHMAN PAINED BY "DAGGER IN THE HEART" FINISH.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-LEHMAN PAINED BY "DAGGER IN THE HEART" FINISH.

text.p: British Open champion Tom Lehman will take a long time to forget the "dagger in the heart" blunder that he feels cost him the U.S. Open title last month.

Though most people recall Lehman hitting his second shot with a seven iron into the water at the 17th hole of the Congressional Course and taking a bogey, the American feels he lost the title a hole earlier.

It was a seven-iron approach at the 16th that he feels hurt him more. It missed the green and finished in an almost impossible position in the rough, from where he could only chip to 15 feet. He two-putted there for bogey.
"The bogey at 16 was the dagger in the heart. It meant that at 17 I had to be aggressive," Lehman said on Tuesday, adding that missing short putts at the 10th and 11th hurt him too.
Lehman led going into the final round, but faltered in the run home to finish third two strokes behind winner Ernie Els.

The popular American lines up on Wednesday in the Loch Lomond World Invitational at the sparkling new course beside the famous Scottish lake as he prepares to defend the British Open title he won at Royal Lytham last year.
He felt he could have won the U.S. Open the last two years, "but you always feel that way when you are close," he said. He was third last month after tying for second last year at Oakland Hills.
"I left Oakland Hills last year, even though I had lost, feeling great about my game," he recalled on Tuesday.
"I felt that except for a couple bounces I could have won. I had great confidence in my game and I felt very excited coming over here.
"Then I saw Royal Lytham and it was love at first sight."
He won by two shots from Mark McCumber and Els.

He feels his game is solid again despite another close U.S. Open defeat. "It's not 100 percent but it's close," he said. "I'd love to be in contention this week, to feel the nerves from being in the hunt.
"That would be a goal achieved. To win would be frosting on the cake," he added.
But he cannot help thinking beyond this weekend to his defence at Royal Troon next week.
He played the course last autumn and was impressed by its toughness.
"I liked the fact that the back nine is so difficult," he said. "From the 10th to the 18th, if you are not solid right through your game it is going to be very rough."
